When you use a command, the user will respond with "Response: " followed by the output of the commmand. Use this output to help the user complete their request.

We encourage testing a large range of inputs before writing a description.

[DESCRIPTION]: Describe what the function is doing in language.

I'll start by testing the function with a variety of inputs to understand its behavior. Let me begin with some simple strings and edge cases.

Interesting - it seems to be mostly identity so far. Let me test with special characters, punctuation, and other cases.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "hello world" "hello!" "hello?" "a.b" "a,b" "a-b" "a_b" "A" "z" "Z" "0" "9" "@" "#" "hello@world.com")

Response: Function input - output pairs: (hello world, world hello) (hello!, hello!) (hello?, hello?) (a.b, a.b) (a,b, a,b) (a-b, a-b) (a_b, a_b) (A, A) (z, z) (Z, Z) (0, 0) (9, 9) (@, @) (#, #) (hello@world.com, hello@world.com)

Now I see something - "hello world" became "world hello" (words swapped). Let me explore this word-swapping behavior more thoroughly.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "a b" "a b c" "a b c d" "one two three" "foo bar baz" "hello there world" "x y z w" "1 2 3" "the quick brown fox")

Response: Function input - output pairs: (a b, b a) (a b c, c b a) (a b c d, d c b a) (one two three, three two one) (foo bar baz, baz bar foo) (hello there world, world there hello) (x y z w, w z y x) (1 2 3, 3 2 1) (the quick brown fox, fox brown quick the)

Now I see the pattern clearly - it reverses the order of space-separated words. Let me test edge cases with multiple spaces, leading/trailing spaces, and non-word characters.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "a  b" "a   b" " a b " "a b " " a b" "a b c d e" "hello world foo" "  " "a	b" "a-b c-d")
Response: Function input - output pairs: (a  b, b a) (a   b, b a) ( a b , b a) (a b , b a) ( a b, b a) (a b c d e, e d c b a) (hello world foo, foo world hello) (  , ) (a	b, b a) (a-b c-d, c-d a-b)

It splits on whitespace (including tabs and multiple spaces) and reverses the word order, then joins with single spaces. Let me verify a few more edge cases - empty strings, newlines, and confirm the joining behavior.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "a b  c   d" "one" "  hello   world  " "a
b" "tab	separated	words")

Response: Function input - output pairs: (a b  c   d, d c b a) (one, one) (  hello   world  , world hello) (a
b, b a) (tab	separated	words, words separated tab)

I now have a clear understanding. Let me confirm the behavior with a final test to be sure about how empty/whitespace-only inputs are handled.

COMMAND: PYTHON(./temp/function.py "" "   " "a" " a " "a b")
Response: Function input - output pairs: (, ) (   , ) (a, a) ( a , a) (a b, b a)

I have enough information to describe the function.

[DESCRIPTION]: The function splits the input string on any whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines, and multiple consecutive whitespace characters), then reverses the order of the resulting non-empty tokens, and joins them back together with a single space. Essentially, it reverses the order of the "words" in the string. If the input is empty or contains only whitespace, the output is an empty string. Single words are returned unchanged (though surrounding whitespace is stripped).

[CODE]:
```python
def f(x):
    return " ".join(reversed(x.split()))
```
